```{r, include = FALSE}

  collapse = TRUE,
  comment = "#>",
  fig.align = "center"
)
has_gt <- requireNamespace("gt", quietly = TRUE)
```

```{r setup}
library(cohortflow)
dat <- mock_parallel_rct(n_participants = 300, seed = 2024)
```

A criteria pipeline is an ordered list of steps. This article covers what a
step can say, how labels and categories appear in reports, how missing
values are handled, and the step types for grouped data.

## Step types at a glance

| Builder | Acts on | Keeps | Typical use |
|---|---|---|---|
| `include()` | each row | rows where the condition is `TRUE` | "Aged 18 or over" |
| `exclude()` | each row | rows where the condition is not `TRUE` | "Withdrew consent" |
| `group_include()` | each group (`by`) | every row of groups where the condition is `TRUE` | "Cluster recruited 20 or more" |
| `group_exclude()` | each group (`by`) | every row of groups where the condition is not `TRUE` | "Site closed early" |
| `select_within()` | rows within each group (`by`) | rows where the condition is `TRUE` within their group | "First admission per patient" |
| `randomise()` | nothing | every row | marks the allocation point |

Steps run in order, and each one sees only the rows that survived the steps
before it. Changing the order changes the counts, so put the steps in the
order your protocol describes.

## Writing conditions

### Formulas

Most conditions are one-sided formulas. Column names are used directly, as
in `dplyr::filter()`:

```{r}
cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ age >= 18 & age < 80, label = "Aged 18 to 79") |>
  include(~ sex %in% c("F", "M"), label = "Sex recorded as F or M")
```

A name that is not a column is looked up where the formula was written, so
thresholds can live in ordinary variables. If a variable and a column share
a name, use the `.data` and `.env` pronouns to say which you mean:

```{r}
min_age <- 18
crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ age >= min_age, label = "Adult") |>
  include(~ .data$age >= .env$min_age, label = "Adult (explicit)")
```

### Functions

A condition can also be a function that takes the data frame and returns a
logical vector, one value per row. Functions suit conditions that are
reused or too long for a formula:

```{r}
is_adult <- function(d) !is.na(d$age) & d$age >= 18

cf_criteria() |>
  include(is_adult, label = "Adult")
```

In printed pipelines, `[~]` marks a formula and `[f]` a function. Formulas
can be checked before any data is touched (see
[Catching mistakes early](#catching-mistakes-early)) and always survive a
round trip to YAML; functions are more flexible but can't be checked, and
complex closures may not survive the round trip.

## Labels and categories

Every step needs a `label`. It names the step in printed flows,
attrition tables and diagrams. A `category` groups consecutive steps under
one heading.

```{r}
crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent")

flow <- apply_criteria(dat, crit, id = "participant_id")
```

Here is where each label ends up in the diagram:

```{r, fig.width = 5.9, fig.height = 3.8, fig.alt = "CONSORT diagram with an Age category box listing its two steps as exclusion reasons, followed by Passed screening and Withdrew consent boxes."}
as_consort_diagram(flow)
```

- A **main box** shows the label of the step (or category) and the number
  remaining *after* it.
- A **side box** shows how many that step removed. For a categorised step it
  also lists each step's label with its own count.

Both places use the same label, so it needs to make sense in both. Short,
neutral descriptions of the condition ("Age recorded", "Consent") usually
work best. If you need different wording in a report, the attrition tibble
is plain data you can relabel.

Categories only group *consecutive* steps, because reordering steps would
change the counts. If a category's steps are split up, cohortflow warns and
reports them as separate groups:

```{r}
split_crit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded", category = "Age") |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over", category = "Age")

tbl <- as_attrition_tibble(apply_criteria(dat, split_crit, id = "participant_id"))
```

Set `show_categories = FALSE` in any report function to show one row per
step instead.

## Missing values

A condition can evaluate to `NA`, for example `age >= 18` when `age` is
missing. The two row-wise step types treat `NA` differently:

- `include()` treats `NA` as *failing*: the row is **removed**.
- `exclude()` treats `NA` as *not matching*: the row is **kept**.

Both are reasonable defaults, but they give different cohorts. In this
dataset 15 people have no recorded age. Compare two ways of writing "adults
only":

```{r}
as_include <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over")
as_exclude <- cf_criteria() |>
  exclude(~ age < 18, label = "Under 18")

flow_inc <- apply_criteria(dat, as_include, id = "participant_id")
flow_exc <- apply_criteria(dat, as_exclude, id = "participant_id")

c(include = nrow(cohort(flow_inc)), exclude = nrow(cohort(flow_exc)))
```

The `include()` version removed the 15 people with missing age along with
the 6 under-18s; the `exclude()` version kept them. Neither is wrong, but
the reported denominator differs, and nothing in either table says why.

The fix is to state the intent. Either handle `NA` in the condition itself:

```{r, eval = FALSE}
include(~ !is.na(age) & age >= 18, label = "Adult with age recorded")
exclude(~ is.na(withdrew) | withdrew, label = "Withdrew or status unknown")
```

or, better for reporting, give missing data its own step so it gets its own
line in the table and diagram:

```{r}
explicit <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over")

as_attrition_tibble(apply_criteria(dat, explicit, id = "participant_id"))
```

To see the raw `TRUE`/`FALSE`/`NA` value of each condition for every row,
use `criteria_status()` with `mode = "independent"`:

```{r}
status <- criteria_status(flow_exc, mode = "independent")
table(`Under 18` = status[["Under 18"]], useNA = "ifany")
```

Grouped steps (below) have one more rule: a row whose `by` column is `NA`
can't be placed in a group, so grouped steps always remove it.

## Grouped data

### Whole groups: `group_include()` and `group_exclude()`

These evaluate the condition once per group, like `dplyr::summarise()`, and
keep or drop *every row* in the group. The condition must return a single
`TRUE` or `FALSE` per group, so it uses summary functions such as `n()`,
`mean()` or `any()`.

Here, in a cluster-randomised trial, clusters are only kept if at least 25
of their participants consented:

```{r}
cl <- mock_cluster_rct(seed = 1)

crit_cl <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(consent_date), label = "Consented") |>
  group_include(by = "cluster_id", ~ n() >= 25,
                label = "Cluster has 25 or more consented") |>
  group_exclude(by = "cluster_id", ~ mean(withdrew) > 0.05,
                label = "Cluster withdrawal over 5%")

apply_criteria(cl, crit_cl, id = "participant_id")
```

Note the order: the cluster-size rule counts only the people who survived
the "Consented" step. Applied first, it would count everyone. The
[Hierarchical and cluster designs](hierarchical-designs.html) article shows
how to report these losses as clusters as well as participants.

### Rows within groups: `select_within()`

`select_within()` evaluates its condition *within* each group and keeps the
rows where it is `TRUE`. It is the natural way to pick one record per person,
such as the index admission or the first period of a crossover trial:

```{r}
co <- mock_crossover(n_participants = 120, seed = 1)

crit_first <- cf_criteria() |>
  select_within(by = "participant_id", ~ period == min(period),
                label = "First period only")

apply_criteria(co, crit_first, id = "event_id")
```

`by` takes several columns for a composite key, for example
`by = c("cluster_id", "period")` for each cluster-period of a stepped-wedge
trial.

## The randomisation point

`randomise()` records where allocation happens: the randomisation unit
(`by`) and the column holding the allocated arm (`arms`). It removes nobody,
but the reporting functions use it:

- `as_consort_diagram()` splits into one column per arm at that point, so
  later exclusions are reported per arm.
- `as_attrition_table()` and `as_attrition_tibble()` break the final count
  down by arm.
- `as_attrition_tibble()` adds a `post_randomisation` column marking steps
  at or after allocation. Exclusions after randomisation can bias the
  comparison, so reviewers look for them specifically.

```{r}
cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ eligible_screen, label = "Passed screening") |>
  randomise(by = "participant_id", arms = "arm") |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew after allocation")
```

For cluster randomisation, use the cluster column as `by`.

## Catching mistakes early

Before any step runs, `apply_criteria()` checks that every formula only uses
columns that exist. A typo or a forgotten join fails straight away and
names the steps involved, instead of failing halfway through with
`object 'x' not found`:

```{r, error = TRUE}
crit_typo <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(bmi), label = "BMI recorded") |>
  exclude(~ smoker, label = "Current smoker")

apply_criteria(dat, crit_typo, id = "participant_id")
```

Run the same check yourself with `check_criteria(criteria, data)`, for
example in a test that the criteria still match the latest data extract.

## Building pipelines from pieces

Pipelines combine with `c()` and subset with `[`, so shared blocks of
criteria can be defined once and reused across analyses:

```{r}
screening <- cf_criteria() |>
  include(~ !is.na(age), label = "Age recorded") |>
  include(~ age >= 18, label = "Aged 18 or over")

follow_up <- cf_criteria() |>
  exclude(~ withdrew, label = "Withdrew consent")

full <- c(screening, follow_up)
length(full)
full[2:3]
```

To add steps to a flow that has *already been applied*, for example once new
data arrives, use `continue_criteria()`, covered in
[Staged pipelines and missing units](https://mattmoo.github.io/cohortflow/articles/staged-pipelines.html).
